text.p: Bangladesh came to a virtual halt on Tuesday as most of the the nation's Moslems responded to a general strike called by radical Islamic groups.
Available transport was limited to a few rickshaws, while offices and schools were closed. Businesses were also expected to be widely affected.

The Islamists called the dawn-to-dusk strike across the country, where nearly 90 percent of its 120 million people are Moslems, to protest against what they regard as attempts to "ridicule and defame" the Prophet Mohammad.
Religious tensions were sparked in Bangladesh after a right-wing Jewish woman in the Israeli town of Hebron plastered storefronts two weeks ago with posters portraying Mohammad as a pig.
Moslem feelings were also hurt after Palestinians said Israeli troops ransacked the al-Yaacoubia school and tore up copies of the Koran.
"The strike is intended to voice our strongest protest against attempts to ridicule the Prophet by blasphemous acts of an Israeli Jewish woman," said a leader of the Jamaat-e-Islami party.
"True Moslems can never tolerate the outrageous act and the devilish courage to dishonour (Prophet) Mohammad," a leader of the radical Islamic Constitution Movement said.
Extra police and paramilitary troops have been deployed in Dhaka and rest of the country to try to prevent violence during Tuesday's stoppage.
Hundreds of angry Islamists on Monday burned Israeli flags in Dhaka and called for a "Jihad (Islamic holy war) against the Jews".
Pro-strike activists on Monday night exploded dozens of home-made bombs in the city. Police said no one was injured.
The main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) led by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia and the Jatiya Party of former military ruler Hossain Mohammad Ershad supported the strike.

The ruling Awami League -- and a few smaller Islamic groups -- opposed the strike, saying that it was unwarranted after the Bangladesh parliament adopted a unanimous resolution condemning the blasphemy.
Awami leader Amir Hossain Amu said on Monday the proponents of the strike had other motives to pursue under a pro-Islamic cover.
